lower-canada.title: Political exclusion and change in Lower Canada
lower-canada.place: Lower Canada, including Trois-Rivières; not present-day Ontario
facts: Ezekiel Hart, a Jewish businessman, was elected to the Lower Canada assembly in 1807 but was not allowed to take his seat.
His sons Samuel Bécancour and Aaron Ezekiel sought change through petitions in 1828 and 1831. Legislation in 1832 extended civil and political rights to Jews in Lower Canada.
lower-canada.interpretation: Explain the religious exclusion and the family’s political action and contribution to change. A law changing eligibility does not prove all prejudice disappeared.

community-hospital.title: Toronto community organising and public care
facts: Jewish women, including Dorothy Dworkin and the Ezras Noshem society, organised and raised funds for a hospital responding to community care needs.

A predecessor opened in 1922 and Mount Sinai Hospital opened in 1923. Jewish physicians faced employment exclusion, while some patients needed care in familiar languages and with familiar dietary practices.
The institution was open to people of all religions. Its contribution to public care did not make Jewish people more entitled to rights than anyone else.
community-hospital.interpretation: Explain a specific community response to exclusion and care needs, and a contribution beyond the founding community. This is Toronto Mount Sinai, not similarly named hospitals elsewhere.

refugee-refusal.title: Canadian refugee exclusion and Holocaust consequences
refugee-refusal.place: Canada and Europe; the ship did not dock in Canada
facts: The Holocaust was Nazi-led systematic persecution and genocide of Jews in Europe; Canada’s antisemitic and restrictive immigration climate made refuge difficult.
In 1939 Canada refused admission to Jewish refugees on the St. Louis. After return to Europe, some passengers were later murdered in the Holocaust; others survived.
Holocaust survivors later settled in Canadian communities and helped shape Canadian life. Their experiences are not represented by an invented first-person account.
refugee-refusal.interpretation: Distinguish the genocide committed by Nazi Germany and collaborators from Canada’s responsibility for its own refugee-exclusion policy. Do not describe all Canadians identically or make suffering the only dimension of Jewish Canadian history.

postwar-rights.title: International post-war commitments and Canadian protection
facts: After the Second World War and Holocaust, international efforts including the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights stated universal rights and helped influence later Canadian protections.
The 1960 Canadian Bill of Rights is a federal statute; the 1977 Canadian Human Rights Act addresses discrimination within its defined federal employment/service scope.
The Charter became part of Canada’s Constitution in 1982; its equality provisions took effect in 1985. Provincial and territorial laws also protect against discrimination in many everyday settings.
International principles, legislation and community action are related developments, not proof that antisemitism ended or that every law has the same reach.

The Canadian Human Rights Commission handles discrimination complaints within its federal jurisdiction; a separate tribunal can hold hearings and order remedies in cases referred to it. Provincial/territorial systems address many everyday employment, housing and service settings. These are concrete response mechanisms, not proof discrimination has ended.
postwar-rights.interpretation: Explain a supported international-to-Canadian influence and distinguish principles, specific protections and continuing problems. No exhaustive legal inventory or real legal-case ruling is required.

fictionalComparison.scenario: A visitor meets the stated eligibility requirements for a public service provided by a federal government department. A staff member refuses that service explicitly because the visitor is Jewish. This is an original fictional example, not a reported case or a legal judgment.
questions: How does the general 1948 universal-rights principle differ from a Canadian law and a complaint-handling route that may apply here?
What are the distinct roles of the Commission and tribunal, and why is a remedy not automatic from making an allegation?
How would checking jurisdiction matter if a different example involved a private local shop? Why would the existence of protection not prove all discrimination ended?
fictionalComparison.limits: Do not decide a real case, guarantee an outcome, demand every legal ground or a complete filing procedure, or portray the general declaration as a Canadian court order.
